objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.line: Virginia's House of Burgesses resolved to petition the King, the Lords and the Commons, saying colonists should be taxed only by representatives they chose.
objects.about: On 14 November 1764 the Virginia House of Burgesses resolved to send an address to the King and memorials to Parliament. It said laws on the colony's internal government and taxes should not be imposed by any power other than the colonists' own representatives. It also said Virginians were already heavily taxed after the late war.

objects.title: Declaration and Resolves
objects.author: First Continental Congress
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.line: The First Continental Congress declared that colonists were entitled to life, liberty and property, and to make their own tax laws in colonial legislatures.
objects.about: The First Continental Congress adopted this declaration in Philadelphia on 14 October 1774. Delegates from twelve colonies listed what Parliament had done, including taxes, the Boston port act and standing armies in peacetime. They resolved that colonists were entitled to life, liberty and property, and to make their own laws on taxation. They also chose peaceful measures, starting with a non-importation agreement.

objects.title: Slaughterhouse Cases - SCOTUS
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.line: The Supreme Court upheld a Louisiana slaughterhouse monopoly, ruling that the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments were passed to give former slaves full equality.
objects.about: In 1873 the Supreme Court ruled on a Louisiana law that gave one New Orleans company a slaughterhouse monopoly. Butchers who lost their trade sued under the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Court upheld the law. It read the amendments as meant mainly to secure equality for former slaves and limited the Privileges or Immunities Clause to rights tied to the federal government.

objects.title: Munn v. Illinois
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.source: Hofstadter, Great Issues in American History
objects.line: The Supreme Court ruled that Illinois could cap rates charged by grain warehouses and elevators, since states may regulate property serving the public good.
objects.about: The Supreme Court decided this case in 1877. Illinois had set maximum rates that grain warehouses and elevators could charge. The owners said the rates denied them equal protection and due process under the 14th Amendment. The Court disagreed. Chief Justice Waite wrote that states may regulate private property "when such regulation becomes necessary for the public good."

objects.title: Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission
objects.author: SCOTUS
objects.about: In Masterpiece Cakeshop, decided 4 June 2018, a Colorado baker named Jack Phillips had declined to make a wedding cake for a same-sex couple because of his religious beliefs. Colorado's civil rights bodies ruled against him. The Supreme Court reversed 7 to 2. It held that commission members showed hostility toward his beliefs, which broke the Free Exercise Clause.
